record.paper_title: Open Questions about Time and Self-reference in Living Systems
record.context_brief: game theory with changing numbers of selves
record.original_question: What mathematics can describe game-theoretic systems in which the number of players or selves changes in real time as a function of the players’ actions, such as biological tissues that can merge, split, or generate new individual decision-makers?

evidence.quote:
One approach that needs to be developed is game theory in which the number of players not only
changes, but changes as a function of the actions of the players.

Depending on what it does, 1 or 2 individuals will result, and the calculus of decision-making will
change because its actions not only change its rewards and what happens, but also change the number
of individuals that exist and make decisions.

To our knowledge,
the mathematics needed to understand the behavior of systems that are self-modifying in the sense of
adding or removing selves in real time does not yet exist.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Develop a mathematical framework for game-theoretic systems in which the set of players is itself a dynamical variable that evolves in real time as a function of the players' actions. Concretely, formulate a model with the following ingredients:

(i) A time-indexed finite (or countable) set of agents N(t), each agent i ∈ N(t) endowed with a state x_i(t) in some measurable space X, an action a_i(t) chosen from an action set A_i(t), and a payoff/utility functional U_i depending on the trajectory of states, actions, and the population history.

(ii) Population-changing operations driven by the agents' actions: birth (creation of a new agent with inherited or initialized state and utility), death (removal of an agent), merging (two or more agents fuse into a single agent whose state, action set, and utility are determined by an aggregation rule), and splitting (one agent fissions into several agents whose states, action sets, and utilities are determined by a partition rule). The rates or triggers of these operations are functions of the current profile of actions and states.

(iii) A consistent notion of strategy and equilibrium that accounts for the fact that an agent's decision can change not only its own future payoff but also the cardinality and identity of the set of decision-makers that will exist and continue choosing actions, including possibly the agent itself ceasing to exist or being replaced by multiple successors.

The problem is to construct such a framework — specifying the appropriate state space, the dynamics of N(t), well-posed strategy spaces, an equilibrium concept (analogous to Nash, correlated, or evolutionarily stable equilibria) that is well-defined under variable player count, and existence/characterization theorems — and to demonstrate its applicability to systems such as biological tissues whose constituent decision-making units can merge, split, or generate new individuals as a result of their own actions.
artifact.status_search_result: No standard mathematical framework appears to exist for games where the number of players changes endogenously as a function of players' actions, including merging and splitting of agents. Related but distinct theories (evolutionary games, mean-field games, population games, branching processes with control) handle exogenous or aggregate population dynamics rather than action-driven creation/destruction of individual decision-makers. The problem is posed as an open direction for which the requisite mathematics has not yet been developed.

status_evidence.title: Population games and evolutionary dynamics (Sandholm)
status_evidence.snippet: Population games study large populations of anonymous agents with fixed total mass; player count is not action-dependent.
status_evidence.claim: Existing population/evolutionary game theory does not model endogenous, action-driven changes in the number of decision-makers.

status_evidence.title: Mean field games (Lasry–Lions)
status_evidence.snippet: Mean field games consider a continuum of players with fixed measure; the population is not created or destroyed by individual actions.
status_evidence.claim: Mean-field game theory does not address action-driven splitting/merging of agents.
